Reproduction & extension · arXiv:2603.10148

Social Knowledge for Cross-Domain User Preference Modeling

I re-implemented the paper's experiments from the released data and SocialVec embeddings, checked every reported number, and extended the evaluation to less popular entities, where a one-size-fits-all popularity ranking has the least to offer.

No user follows more than 5,000 accounts, which looks like a limit of the data collection.

How the LLM prompts are built

The personalized prompts use the authors' wording and list the names of accounts the user follows. The names are the accounts' Twitter display names, as recorded in the SocialVec account metadata (not their handles); accounts without a recorded name are dropped from the list, so a prompt can list fewer accounts than its k. The accounts are drawn at random with a fixed seed (the same draw for a user wherever the condition appears) and listed in the order drawn, which is random:

  • k = 12 and k = 25: drawn from the user's closed set, the candidate entities of the other categories' lists that the user follows (the paper's "favored entities"). The target category's own entities are never in this set.
  • k = 50: drawn from everything the user follows. In Table 3, as in the paper, the target category's own candidates can be among them (see Section 2); in Table 9–Table 11 and Section 5, every listed entity of the target category is removed before drawing.

The candidates to rank are given as a JSON list of ids and names. Where they appear in random order is summarized in Table 14 (Section 4).

Table 3 · LLM personalization per category, paper Table 3

I re-ran the LLM experiment with GPT-6 Luna (reasoning effort low) and the authors' prompts, on a stratified random sample of 50 users per category. The paper's finding replicates: listing 12 favored entities lifts MAP from 0.452 to 0.542 (+20%), and 50 accounts lift it to 0.603 (+33%). The paper reported +13% and +23% for GPT-4o. The social-embedding column (SE1, k = 50) matches the paper on all users: 0.562 vs. 0.562. On the same 700 users, SocialVec scores 0.507 with the 12 accounts and 0.511 with the 25 accounts listed in the LLM prompts (k = 50: 0.559), so the LLM is ahead at 12 and 25 accounts, as it is at ranks 81–100 (Table 9).

2Notes on the original code

Things I found while matching the notebooks. None of them changes the paper's conclusions.

Bug

Target entities were never removed

The "All" profile subtracts screen names from a set of numeric ids, which removes nothing, so the target category stays in the profile. Removing it properly moves overall MAP from 0.621 to 0.617 (+24% → +24%).

Sampling

SE1 samples can't be redrawn exactly

The original order came from a set of string ids, which changes with every Python run. Redrawn with the same seed, the overall values land within ±0.004. The closed-world (SE2) samples match exactly.

Detail

"Entities" are followed accounts

SE1 samples k followed accounts, and only about 43% of them are SocialVec entities. The paper's "1,972 entities per user" counts all followed accounts.

3Extension · Less popular entities

Does social user modeling still help when the candidates aren't the most famous entities in their category?

In the 9 categories that list 100 typed entities, I sorted the entities by Twitter follower count and ranked those at positions 81–100 instead of the top 20. No original sheet lists more. User profiles exclude every entity known to belong to the target category: its original sheet, its top-20 list and its extended list, so none of the 40 candidates (ranks 1–20 and 81–100) is in any profile. The main setup (Table 6) evaluates each of the 11,153 users in every category in which they follow at least one entity of the band; as a matched control, the original top 20 are ranked for the same users with the same profiles. Table 5 repeats this for only the users sampled for each category. A random ranking (exact expected AP) provides a chance level, and paired Wilcoxon tests compare the two methods.

  • Popularity breaks down in the tail. On all 36,739 user–category pairs, at ranks 81–100 it scores 0.291, barely above a random ranking (0.252), and below it for News outlets, Politicians, TV stations and Journalists.
  • Social similarity holds up. It scores 0.400, above chance in 9 of 9 categories, and beats popularity in 8 of 9. Its relative gain over popularity grows from +23% on the top 20 to +37% (p < 0.001 overall and in every category).
  • The matched control on the users sampled for each category agrees. On those 3,798 users the gain is +22% on the top 20 and +38% at ranks 81–100 (Table 5).
  • The exception is Comedians (−23%). Follows in that band concentrate on its two most-followed accounts, both mainly political commentators, which popularity ranks first.

How popular are the candidates overall?

The bands are defined within each category. To see where the candidates stand among all accounts, I placed every candidate in the popularity ranking of all 201,346 SocialVec accounts, which are sorted by how many users follow them (rank 1 is the most followed). In these 9 categories, the original top 20 have a median global rank of 405; the ranks 81–100 candidates 13,672, with 38% of them in the global top 10,000.

Table 9 · LLM and SocialVec ranking of ranks 81–100

The Table 3 protocol applied to the less popular candidates, for 200 random users per category who follow at least one candidate (1,798 users; TV stations have only 198). Every listed entity of the target category is removed from the prompts. Without user information, the LLM is no better than popularity (0.284 vs. 0.297). With user information it personalizes well: 0.392 with 12 entities and 0.480 with 50 accounts. Social similarity from all of the user's entities scores 0.418. The two are complementary: with 12 entities the LLM is stronger for news outlets, comedians, politicians and journalists; social similarity from all entities for musical artists, TV stations, actors, TV shows and sports teams.

For a like-for-like comparison, the SocialVec k = 12 and k = 25 columns build the user embedding from exactly the accounts listed in the LLM's k = 12 and k = 25 prompts (11.7 and 21.7 on average, as some users have fewer). Follow statistics of these 1,798 users: accounts followed: minimum 68, mean 2,256, median 1,950, maximum 5,000; candidate entities followed: minimum 11, mean 48.4, median 44, maximum 170. Given the same evidence, the LLM ranks better at both sizes: 0.392 vs. 0.354 with 12 accounts (paired Wilcoxon p < 0.001; ahead in 6 of 9 categories), and 0.394 vs. 0.352 with 25 (p < 0.001; ahead in 7 of 9).

Table 10 · LLM and SocialVec ranking, ranks 1–20 vs. 81–100 (same users)

The protocol of Table 9 repeated on the 20 most popular candidates of each category, for the 1,751 users of Table 9 who follow at least one of them. Unlike Table 3, every listed entity of the target category is removed from the prompts here too, so the two bands differ only in their candidates. Among the most popular candidates, popularity is a strong ranking (0.553), and the LLM without user information beats it (0.591). Given the same accounts, the LLM is ahead of SocialVec in both bands: 0.671 vs. 0.630 with 12 accounts at ranks 1–20 (p < 0.001; ahead in 9 of 9 categories).

Limitations

Only the original top-20 candidates were manually validated; the lower ranks include some mistyped entities (esports teams among sports teams, party accounts among TV stations). Users were sampled as followers of the top-20 entities. Users follow only 1.4–5.6 band candidates each, so per-user AP is noisy in the smaller categories.

4Does the LLM depend on the order of the candidates?

The original prompts list the candidates sorted by follower count, which an order-following model could turn into popularity ranking for free.

For the same 700 users, I re-ran the k = 25 prompts twice: once unchanged, to measure run-to-run noise, and once with the candidates shuffled. I also called the non-personalized baseline 10 times per category in its original order and 10 times shuffled. The results are in Table 12 and Table 13.

  • Personalization barely depends on the order. Shuffling lowers MAP from 0.554 to 0.541. The drop is significant (p < 0.001) but small, and repeating the identical prompt gives 0.553.
  • Some of the popularity signal comes from the input order. The output's correlation with popularity falls from τ = 0.32 to 0.20 when the candidates are shuffled.
  • The non-personalized baseline follows the input order more closely (τ = 0.51). Shuffling costs it 0.022 MAP, several times the spread across repeated calls. Non-personalized LLM rankings should be evaluated with randomized orders.
  • Outputs are not deterministic. Ten identical baseline calls gave 9.9 distinct rankings on average. Two identical personalized calls change a user's AP by 0.058 on average, but overall MAP is stable.

5Can demographics alone personalize the LLM?

The second version of this experiment, on the users of Table 9–Table 11 and with a one-value-per-attribute instruction. The first version (270 users) is in results.html and the demographics report.

GPT-4o first guessed each user's gender, age, ethnicity and education from the names of accounts they follow, and was told to rely on stereotypes rather than decline and to state exactly one value per attribute. GPT-6 Luna then ranked the candidates given only that description, both for the most popular candidates of each category (ranks 1–20, as in Table 3) and for ranks 81–100; Claude Haiku 5.5 repeated every ranking (same users, candidate orders, descriptions and prompts) as a second, low-cost ranking model. Every ranking lists the candidates in one random order per user, shared by all of that user's conditions. For comparison, the same shuffled candidates were also ranked from the names of 12, 25 or 50 followed accounts.

Prompts

Both stages use dspy signatures, as in the original experiments. These are the exact messages dspy sends, with the inputs shown as placeholders in braces. The last instruction of Stage 1 is new in this version.

Stage 1 · Generating the demographic description (GPT-4o)

── system message ──
Your input fields are:
1. `followed_accounts` (str): Names of accounts the user follows
Your output fields are:
1. `description` (str): One or two sentences stating the user's most likely gender, age, ethnicity, and level of education
All interactions will be structured in the following way, with the appropriate values filled in.

[[ ## followed_accounts ## ]]
{followed_accounts}

[[ ## description ## ]]
{description}

[[ ## completed ## ]]
In adhering to this structure, your objective is: 
Given the names of accounts that a Twitter user follows, write a short, concise description of the user that states their most likely gender, age, ethnicity, and level of education (primary school, high school, higher education, etc.).
Deduce these attributes only from the names of the accounts they follow.
You must always guess the most likely value of all four attributes, based on stereotypes about the typical audience of these accounts, even when the evidence is weak. Never answer that the attributes cannot be determined or that the evidence is insufficient.
Describe only these four attributes: do not mention the user's interests or hobbies, and do not name any of the accounts.
State exactly one value for each attribute: one gender, one age group (for example "in their 30s"), one ethnicity and one level of education. Never give a range spanning two groups or alternatives such as "30s or 40s" or "Caucasian or mixed".

── user message ──
[[ ## followed_accounts ## ]]
{names of up to 50 accounts the user follows, comma-separated}

Respond with the corresponding output fields, starting with the field `[[ ## description ## ]]`, and then ending with the marker for `[[ ## completed ## ]]`.

Stage 2 · Ranking the candidates from the description (GPT-6 Luna)

── system message ──
Your input fields are:
1. `user_description` (str): Short description of the user's gender, age, ethnicity, and level of education
2. `potential_accounts` (str): JSON list of potential accounts to recommend with twitter_user_id and names
Your output fields are:
1. `ranked_ids` (str): list with the account twitter_user_id sorted by priority as a ranked key
All interactions will be structured in the following way, with the appropriate values filled in.

[[ ## user_description ## ]]
{user_description}

[[ ## potential_accounts ## ]]
{potential_accounts}

[[ ## ranked_ids ## ]]
{ranked_ids}

[[ ## completed ## ]]
In adhering to this structure, your objective is: 
given the below Twitter user, for whom we provide a short demographic description, and a list of possible accounts to recommend for the user to follow, create a prioritized recommendation list.
You must rank the entire list provided to you.
Try to deduce what you think the user might like based on their demographic description.
Return ONLY a valid list object with the ranked account twitter_user_id sorted by relevance (highest to lowest). Do not include name or reasoning.
Example format: [71026122, 141341662, 567562934, ...]

── user message ──
[[ ## user_description ## ]]
{the description written by GPT-4o}

[[ ## potential_accounts ## ]]
{JSON list of the candidates: twitter_user_id and twitter_name}

Respond with the corresponding output fields, starting with the field `[[ ## ranked_ids ## ]]`, and then ending with the marker for `[[ ## completed ## ]]`.

The model's answer is read from the [[ ## ranked_ids ## ]] field. The ranking prompts with account names and without user information are the authors' prompts used throughout this page. Claude Haiku 5.5 receives exactly the same system and user messages through the Anthropic API (adaptive thinking at effort low, Message Batches API).

The user follows 6 of the 20 candidates; AP = 0.457.

  • Demographics help, most in the tail. GPT-4o's descriptions beat the no-information ranking at ranks 81–100, 0.340 vs. 0.284 (p < 0.001), and by less at ranks 1–20, 0.619 vs. 0.591 (p < 0.001).
  • Among the most popular candidates the no-information ranking is already strong: 0.591 at ranks 1–20, against popularity's 0.553 (p < 0.001).
  • Account names say more than demographics. 12 names score 0.392 at ranks 81–100 and 0.671 at ranks 1–20, above the descriptions in both (p < 0.001 and < 0.001).
  • 50 names beat SocialVec's full profile: 0.480 vs. 0.417 at ranks 81–100 (p < 0.001) and 0.710 vs. 0.660 at ranks 1–20 (p < 0.001).
  • On the 544 users who pass the follow filter, the demographic gain holds at ranks 81–100 (0.349 vs. 0.283, p < 0.001) but not at ranks 1–20 (0.661 vs. 0.648, p = 0.136); at ranks 81–100 they come close to 12 account names (0.361, p = 0.197).
  • Claude Haiku 5.5 ranks a little lower but shows the same ordering. Demographics beat no information at ranks 81–100, 0.329 vs. 0.273 (p < 0.001), and at ranks 1–20, 0.577 vs. 0.556 (p < 0.001), and account names beat demographics. Unlike GPT-6 Luna, its 50 account names only match SocialVec's full profile: 0.414 vs. 0.418 at ranks 81–100 (p = 0.749) and 0.655 vs. 0.660 at ranks 1–20 (p = 0.994).
  • The descriptions stay on demographics. Only 19 of the 1,798 descriptions also name the user's interests, against the instruction (60 of 270 in the first version).

What GPT-4o stated about the users

Each description is parsed with fixed rules for the value it states for each attribute. With the one-value instruction, 84 attribute values across the 1798 descriptions still name more than one value (174 across 270 in the first version); those count under the first value stated. "Middle-aged" is kept as stated, without assigning it an age range.

  • The guesses are concentrated. 1589 of 1798 descriptions say Caucasian or white and 1696 say higher education without a level. Gender is the most balanced attribute (1057 male, 741 female).

6Open items

Scale

LLM experiments on all users

The LLM results use samples of 50 users per category (200 for ranks 81–100), which keeps overall MAP within about ±0.01. A full-population run takes about 45K calls. The same command runs it with larger samples, and cached responses are reused.

Next

Description-based tail candidates

The requested variant selects 50–100 accounts per category by their textual descriptions, below the top 10K/20K SocialVec entities. The ranks 81–100 band does not meet that criterion fully: 110 of its 177 candidates (62%) fall below the top 10K, and it uses the typed lists rather than descriptions.

Regenerate the underlying results with python run_reproduction.py, python run_popularity_band.py --start 81 --end 100 and python run_llm_experiments.py. For Section 5, run python run_llm_demographics.py (with --describe-model gpt-4o for the repeat), python run_llm_demographics_bands.py and python make_demographics_report.py. Then rebuild this page with python make_results_page.py. Details are in results/REPORT.md, results/POPULARITY_BAND_REPORT.md and results/LLM_REPORT.md. Results that use the extended category lists are kept in results_backup.html.
